steps.say: When the diaphragm fails to close, abdominal organs push into the chest and stunt lung growth. The back side hole dominates, the front hole is next, and middle holes are rare.
steps.tx: A hole in the diaphragm lets belly organs crowd the chest before birth. **Congenital diaphragmatic hernia** (birth hole in the breathing sheet) occurs in about **1 in 2000 to 5000 births** (one in two thousand to five thousand births). **Bochdalek hernia** (back side hole) defects make **70 to 75 percent** (seventy to seventy five percent), anterior **Morgagni hernia** (front hole) makes **23 to 28 percent** (twenty three to twenty eight percent), and central **diaphragmatic defect** (middle hole) makes **2 to 7 percent** (two to seven percent).

vis.alt: Illustration of an infant with diaphragmatic hernia and pulmonary hypoplasia beside covered omphalocele sac and uncovered gastroschisis bowel.
vis.caption: Diaphragmatic hernia with pulmonary hypoplasia, beside covered omphalocele and open gastroschisis. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Most holes sit on the left, yet both lungs grow small with thickened tiny arteries. That high lung blood pressure after birth matters more than the hole itself.
steps.tx: Side and lung damage decide survival. **Bochdalek hernia** (back side hole) is left sided in **85 percent** (eighty five percent), right sided in **13 percent** (thirteen percent) and bilateral in **2 percent** (two percent). Both lungs suffer **lung hypoplasia** (small undergrown lungs) with thickened **arteriolar muscle** (tiny artery wall), which drives **pulmonary hypertension** (high lung blood pressure) after birth, the true killer in this disease.

vis.alt: Illustration of pulmonary hypoplasia with arrested hypoplastic lung, decreased bronchial branching, mediastinal shift, herniated bowel loops and Bochdalek defect.
vis.caption: Bochdalek defect with herniated bowel, hypoplastic lung and mediastinal shift. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Scans from fifteen weeks can spot the shifted chest, stomach bubble beside the heart and excess fluid. A liver in the chest plus heart or chromosome problems warns of a rough course.
steps.tx: The diagnosis usually arrives before birth. **Prenatal ultrasound** (pregnancy scan) from **15 weeks** (fifteen weeks) shows **mediastinal shift** (pushed chest centre), juxtacardiac gastric dilatation and **polyhydramnios** (excess womb water). An intrathoracic liver plus cardiac or chromosomal anomalies predicts poor outcome, so these babies are delivered where ECMO and paediatric surgery stand ready.

steps.say: Doctors measure the good lung against the head size to judge how undergrown the lungs are. That ratio shapes parent counselling and delivery planning.
steps.tx: One ratio guides counselling and delivery planning. The **lung to head ratio** (fetal lung measure) compares the contralateral lung area with head circumference against gestational norms, estimating **fetal lung size** (unborn lung growth). A low ratio predicts early neonatal morbidity and shapes **prognosis** (expected outcome) talks with parents, including where and when to deliver and whether fetal therapy applies.

steps.say: A blue grunting baby with a hollow belly, quiet chest, bowel gurgles above the diaphragm and shifted heartbeats is this disease until proven otherwise. Mask ventilation balloons the stomach, so drop a stomach tube at once.
steps.tx: The delivery room picture is dramatic and classic. The infant shows grunting, retractions and cyanosis with a **scaphoid abdomen** (hollow boat belly), diminished breath sounds, **bowel sounds in chest** (gurgles above the diaphragm) and shifted heart tones, with pre and postductal saturation differences from blood crossing through a **right to left shunt** (bypass flow). Mask ventilation inflates the stomach and worsens the shift, so pass a gastric tube at once.

steps.say: A balloon placed in the windpipe before birth can trap lung fluid and grow the lung, then it is removed before delivery. A landmark trial showed better survival to discharge and six months.
steps.tx: Some lungs can be grown before birth. **FETO** (fetal balloon lung growth) places a tracheal balloon at **27 to 29 weeks** (twenty seven to twenty nine weeks) with later retrieval, trapping lung fluid to drive **lung growth** (unborn lung expansion). The **TOTAL trial** (balloon therapy trial) showed survival benefit at discharge and at **6 months** (six months). It suits severe left sided cases in experienced fetal centres, not every hernia.

steps.say: Do not rush to the theatre. Stable babies are repaired at two to three days when circulation steadies, and babies on heart lung support are often fixed after weaning.
steps.tx: Repair waits for stability, not speed. Stable infants undergo **primary repair** (own tissue closure) at **48 to 72 hours** (forty eight to seventy two hours) to avoid vascular lability, since rushed early operations bleed and crash. Bleeding is worse on ECMO, so some centres repair after weaning. This **timing of repair** (planned delay rule) closes with interrupted nonabsorbable sutures, reserving **Gore-Tex patch** (synthetic sheet) for large defects.

steps.say: Squeezing everything back can choke belly blood flow, so surgeons sometimes close only the skin or stage closure with a sac. Survivors need years of lung, feed, spine, growth and development follow up.
steps.tx: Closing the belly can strangle it, and survival starts lifelong follow up. Returning the organs can lose abdominal domain and cause **abdominal compartment syndrome** (crushed belly circulation) needing a **silo** (staged sac closure) or skin only closure. Survivors carry **long term morbidity** (lasting harm): chronic lung disease, reflux, scoliosis, growth failure and developmental delay, so follow up runs for years.
